title: AssoMem: Scalable Memory QA with Multi-Signal Associative Retrieval
one_liner: Organize conversation memory around linked clues, then rank possible memories using relevance, importance, and timing together instead of semantic similarity alone.
lead: A memory system for question answering has to find the right past moment from a very long conversation. Pure semantic search often fails when many memories sound similar. AssoMem adds structure: it attaches each utterance to extracted clues, builds an associative memory graph, and ranks memories with three signals at once so recall improves in dense conversational histories because the scorer can separate the truly answer-supporting turn from other turns that only share similar wording.

problem.h2: Why similar conversations confuse memory search
paras: A personal assistant may store thousands of dialogue turns. Later, a user asks a question such as who promised to send the draft or when the budget concern first came up. Many stored turns may use similar words, so plain semantic retrieval brings back several plausible but wrong moments.

The problem is not only relevance to the question. Some past turns were central decisions, some were minor side remarks, and some happened at the right time to answer the question while others are stale. A memory search system that treats all three cases the same will often recall the wrong turn.

callout.html: AssoMem links dialogue turns to explicit clues and then ranks memories with relevance, importance, and timing together so the system can recover the right past event from many similar ones.

paras: The paper changes how memories are organized and ranked. Instead of keeping only a flat list of utterances scored by semantic match, it builds an associative graph and fuses several retrieval signals.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: answer usefulness of a memory item
hidden.name: how likely one stored turn is to directly support the answer
paras: The right memory is not simply the one that sounds closest to the question. It is the one that actually helps answer it because it carries the fact, decision, or timing detail the question needs. That depends on at least three factors: does the turn discuss the topic, was the turn important in the conversation, and does its timing fit the question being asked?

AssoMem tries to estimate this hidden usefulness by building links from each utterance to extracted clues and by combining the three signals with a learned fusion rule. The graph matters because it gives the retriever more than raw text similarity to work with when many turns are phrased in similar ways.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark signals that more strongly indicate whether a memory item will support the final answer.

reads.html: The system asks which old turn will actually help answer the current question because that turn contains the fact or decision the answer depends on.
The method builds an associative memory graph and uses adaptive fusion of relevance, importance, and temporal alignment for ranking.

mechanism.h2: Why several signals beat similarity alone
paras: Similarity alone misses conversational role. A side remark can share most of the same words as a key decision turn and still be the wrong memory. Adding importance helps because the system can prefer turns that carried decisions, commitments, or clarifications instead of low-stakes chatter.

Timing also matters because questions often ask about the latest agreement, the first mention, or the turn near another event. The fusion rule combines these signals so that one weak signal does not dominate the ranking. This works because the memory graph stores clue links that expose who, what, and when, allowing the scorer to rank candidate turns using structure instead of wording alone.

math.words: memory score = weighted relevance plus weighted importance plus weighted timing alignment
math.equation: Score(m) = a * Relevance(m) + b * Importance(m) + c * TimeFit(m)
symbols: final retrieval score for memory item m
how directly the memory matches the question topic
how central that turn was in the conversation
how well the timing of the turn fits the question
weights chosen by the fusion method

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Candidate A matches the topic well: relevance 0.9, but it was a minor aside: importance 0.2, and the timing is weak: 0.3.
Candidate B matches the topic slightly less: relevance 0.8, but it was the main decision turn: importance 0.9, and the timing fits well: 0.8.
With weights a = 0.4, b = 0.3, c = 0.3, Candidate A scores 0.51 while Candidate B scores 0.83.
Candidate B wins because the extra signals show it is the turn that actually supports the answer.

math.note: The important idea is not the exact arithmetic. It is that a memory item should win only when several useful signals agree.

items.b: Clue extraction can miss the real anchor.
items.html: If the system fails to extract a key person, date, or commitment, the graph loses the very link that would have separated the right memory from the wrong one.
A brief turn may look unimportant even when it contains the exact decision or correction the answer needs.

items.b: Timing can overwhelm older but critical facts.
items.html: Recent turns are often useful, but some questions ask about an earlier origin or a long-standing promise. If timing is weighted too strongly, the ranking may push those older critical turns too low.
The retrieval score works best when the three signals can counterbalance one another, because then a turn wins for a concrete reason instead of by wording overlap alone.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a dialogue memory benchmark with long meeting transcripts. Ask factual questions whose answers depend on identifying the right past turn among several similar ones. Compare a semantic-only retriever against a system that also scores importance and timing.
For each question, show the top five retrieved turns and mark which one truly supports the answer. Then feed those retrieved turns into the same answer generator.
demo.metric_eq: answer_support_hit = questions where the correct supporting turn appears in top_k / total questions
demo.closing: The demo should show that multi-signal retrieval lifts QA accuracy because it can recover the memory turn that truly supports the answer, not merely the one with the closest wording.
